title: Eikev: not my hand alone (Deuteronomy 8:17–18)
hook: beware saying "my power and the might of my hand" earned this

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manna, and a line the world still quotes. Your line was not by bread alone. What did you feed besides your stomach? Today, what happens after the bread is plentiful. Day four hundred ninety-three.

Listen to almost any success story at a podcast microphone. I started in a garage. I worked eighteen-hour days. Nobody believed in me. It's often true. But the parents who covered rent, the teacher who noticed, the lucky timing, the country with roads and courts, the health that held: they usually get edited out. Not out of malice. Success just tells itself in the first person. Moses saw this coming for a people about to move from tents into houses. In the middle of Eikev he warns them about one sentence they'll be tempted to say.
screen: `I STARTED IN A GARAGE.` → `THE EDITED-OUT HELP.` → `ONE SENTENCE TO WATCH FOR.`

segments.voice: The chapter starts with gratitude. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." That verse is the root of the Jewish grace after meals, birkat hamazon. You eat, you're full, you bless. Then, right away, the warning. When you've eaten and are full, Moses says, and built fine houses, and your herds and silver and gold have multiplied, watch out that your heart doesn't lift itself up and forget. And the sentence: "and thou say in thy heart: 'My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.'" In Hebrew, kochi v'otzem yadi. My strength, and the might of my hand. Then the answer: "But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth." Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say you did nothing, or that work is pointless. Your hand was real. It says the power in the hand came from somewhere. Strength, health, wits, the land itself: given. The danger isn't wealth. It's the sentence, said in your heart, that erases everyone and everything that made the wealth possible. And notice the timing. Not in hunger. The warning comes when you're full. The same full stomach that leads to a blessing can lead to forgetting, and Moses puts the two side by side, a verse apart.
screen: `EAT, BE SATISFIED, AND BLESS.` · `WHEN THE HOUSES ARE BUILT.` · `KOCHI V'OTZEM YADI.` · `WHO GAVE THE POWER?` · then, large: `NOT MY HAND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: credit someone for your success. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're proud of. A degree, a job, a home, a skill, a child who turned out well. Tell its story to yourself in one sentence, the way you'd tell it at a party. Now tell it again, slowly, and let the hidden helpers in. Who paid, taught, waited, covered for you, believed you? What luck did you get? Choose one of them to thank today. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where Moses warns a full people about the sentence my hand did this.
Your line: not my hand alone. Today, when you tell a success story, put one helper back in it, out loud. Day four hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Jews say birkat hamazon, the grace after meals, after eating bread, based on Deuteronomy 8:10, and many teachers pair it with the warning a few verses later against saying my power and the might of my hand.

original.note: Hebrew: my power and the might of my hand. the sentence Moses warns against in Deuteronomy 8:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be arrogant about money.
what it means: the danger isn't wealth but the sentence that erases everyone and everything that made it possible.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 8:10, the source of birkat hamazon, sits a few verses before kochi v'otzem yadi: blessing and forgetting share a full stomach.
